cards.title: Several vulnerabilities have been discovered in the Linux kernel

depth.text: a Debian alert warns **Linux kernel bugs** could **leak information**, disrupt service, or grant extra access
For Debian's **stable distribution**, trixie, the fix is **version 6.12.111-1**; the alert recommends **upgrading Linux packages**.

cards.camps: Some commenters see AI-assisted research driving more vulnerability discoveries; others caution that CVE counts are a poor measure because kernel bugfixes can get CVE numbers too.

comments.text: note that _any_ bugfix is assigned a cve, which makes for big numbers. > “Due to the layer at which the Linux kernel is in a system, almost any bug might be exploitable to compromise the security of the kernel… Because of this, the CVE assignment team is overly cautious and assign CVE numbers to any bugfix that they identify.” https://docs.kernel.org/process/cve.html "number of cves" is a useless…
Just the beginning. AI is going to expose how fragile the entire computing infrastructure in our world is.

An interesting observation that I encountered somewhere, I forget where, is that AIs when writing code introduce vulnerabilities at a rate similar to humans writing the same code. So we're looking at a massively accelerated volume of security vulnerabilities for the foreseeable future thanks to AI-assisted security research, and we can expect no reduction in new vulnerabilities from the AIs…
I thought the "Security in the LLM age" talk by Greg Kroah-Hartman published this week from Kernel Recipes was pretty interesting: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NnV_cWeoo5Q

This is great, more access did provide more eyes on these problems. But, does that all of these being found now call into question, not the open source model logic itself, but the ability of human eyes to find security issues? These vulnerabilities have been sitting here for however long, but how many thousands of humans did not find them before AI?

cards.title: Various Projects Find Hidden SDR Capabilities in ESP32 Microcontrollers

depth.text: someone found a **hidden feature** that lets ESP32 chips capture **raw radio signals**, beyond WiFi and Bluetooth

Several models can capture raw IQ samples across **2.2–2.7 GHz**, with the ESP32-C5 also covering **4.8–6.0 GHz**. For general PC use, most can only export snapshots, but the ESP32-S31 can stream continuously at up to **16 MS/s** over Gigabit Ethernet.

comments.text: So many $1 wireless ICs have a powerful "SDR", but will never be documented due to certification/compiliance/export-control reasons. The projects listed here rightly limited the scope to RX-only but Espressif might be forced to "patch" this away if arbitrary TX too is possible (or starts making headlines). Hope it doesn't come to that, more cheap options for RF-to-bits is always welcome. On a…

As far as I follow the research process it's currently quite difficult to get all data (like the 80MSPS@10-Bit showcase on Reddit) to a computer without a FPGA+USB3. With the new ESP32-S31 we most likely can extract the I/Q data over its new 1 GBit/s interface. Guessing something around 20-40MSPS should work. These hack will most likely will be a revolution for 13cm ham radio. With the new 5GHz…

Very exciting! > However, the current prototype uses the FPGA to clock the ESP32, which results in poor phase noise. Looks like this was solved five days ago: https://github.com/h0m3us3r/eSpDR/commit/41a0ffe279119df942e...

The ESP32S3 support PSRAM, can we redirect the sample to PSRAM, then hooking Logic Analyzer on PSRAM, thus getting the sample directly, not through any digital interface.
(There is cache before PSRAM, but should be trivial to sync).
Any way to finagle a LORA type system (ultra reliable using precise timing) using a few of these on each end?

cards.title: The death of web development education

depth.text: a writer says **AI chatbots** are hollowing out **web development education** and its teachers

Axel Rauschmayer says his **book income** fell to zero, and course creators report **revenue down 50%+**. The author calls for **paid, human-led learning**; commenters disagree over whether chatbots improve education or hollow it out.

cards.camps: Two camps: some say chatbots offer better, more personalized education and people should adapt; others say they let learners skip the learning itself and threaten educators' livelihoods.

cards.title: Automatic Transmission – a data-privacy study of connected vehicles

depth.text: a study found **connected cars** and their apps sending **personal data** to outside companies

Researchers tested **21 vehicles** and **30 companion apps**: 19 vehicles contacted at least one third party over Wi-Fi, and seven apps sent sensitive identifiers to third parties. Pairing an app **roughly doubled** exposure to advertising and tracking companies on average.
data: vehicles contacting a third party over Wi-Fi

cards.camps: Two camps: one commenter says owners can simply stop using connected-vehicle features; another says cars still send telemetry and opting out can be hard or impossible.

comments.text: I currently drive a mid 2000s Ford truck, which runs great and meets my needs, but lately I got interested in minivans/people carriers. I pretty quickly realized that newer vehicles seem to not just record, but export a lot of driving data. The minivan market is small. There are really only 4-5 available and every single one sends telemetry data from the car and makes it hard/impossible to opt…

if an owner decides they are uncomfortable with the data sharing described within them, they are faced with (arguably) unfair choices:
- 01 accept the agreements regardless of their concerns
- 02 stop using their car's connected-vehicle features - which includes remote start, the app, and other very useful features
- 03 stop using the vehicle entirely
Easy, I take #2. Is that it? This whole time…
> As one notable exception, Honda improved its data collection practices to prevent sending precise geolocation to a third party associated with user tracking. I know what my next car will be.

The ongoing theme of all these responses was shifting the blame to the consumer. As expected. I think consumers also need to push back on these practices, but the problem is, majority of consumers are tech savy but not privacy savy.

Hope to see a new market for disabling telemetry and phonehome features from cars. It should be legal to do so, if you own the car I suppose. I'm thinking that rigth now few pople even know how much spying their new car does to them but this will change and as awareness grows more and more people will want to do it.

glossary.CVE: Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures: a standard ID assigned to a publicly known security flaw so people can refer to the same issue.
glossary.privilege escalation: A flaw that lets someone get more control of a computer than they should have.
glossary.denial of service: An attack or flaw that makes a service unavailable to people trying to use it.
glossary.kernel: A small program that carries out a calculation on a computer's graphics chip or processor.
glossary.framework: A collection of ready-made parts and rules that helps people build software.
glossary.type safety: Checks that values are used in ways the code expects, catching some mistakes before the app runs.
glossary.migration: Changing code to work with a newer version, sometimes with steps handled automatically.
glossary.alias: A shorter stand-in name for a longer file path.
glossary.remote functions: Tools for letting an app safely send work to a server and get an answer back.
glossary.Async Svelte: A Svelte capability that remote functions need, and that currently has to be switched on experimentally.
glossary.experimental flag: A setting you turn on to try a feature that isn't ready for ordinary use.
glossary.SDR: Software-defined radio: a radio that uses software to handle signals instead of being limited to one fixed radio function.
glossary.IQ samples: A pair of measurements that records a radio signal’s strength and position in its wave, so software can process it.
glossary.GHz: Gigahertz: a unit for how quickly a radio wave repeats.
glossary.MS/s: Millions of samples per second; it describes how quickly the device captures measurements of a signal.
glossary.GenAI: Generative AI: tools that make new text, images, or code from instructions.
glossary.LLMs: Large language models: computer programs trained on lots of writing that can produce text.
glossary.Developer Relations: A company role focused on helping developers learn about and use its products.
glossary.API reference: A guide to the ways a program can ask another program for information or actions.
glossary.AI crawlers: Automated programs that visit websites and collect their content for AI systems.
glossary.nondeterministic: Able to give different results even when asked the same thing twice.
glossary.agentic: Describes AI that chooses steps and acts toward a task, rather than only answering a question.
glossary.full-stack: Building both the parts of an app people use and the behind-the-scenes parts that make it work.
glossary.Revenue Cycle Management (RCM): The steps a healthcare provider takes to check coverage, bill for care, and collect payment.
glossary.connected vehicle: A car with internet access that can keep communicating with its maker and other companies.
glossary.third party: A company outside the carmaker that receives information from the car or its app.
glossary.telemetry: Information a program sends back about how it is being used or whether it is working properly.
glossary.sensitive identifiers: Personal details that can point to someone or their vehicle, such as an email, phone number, or vehicle ID.
glossary.VIN: Vehicle Identification Number: a number that identifies a particular vehicle.
glossary.Faraday tent: A tent that blocks radio signals; researchers used one to cut off the cars' cellular connections.
glossary.PII: Personally Identifiable Information: details that could identify someone, such as an email or phone number.
